source.title: PURE: Turning Polysemantic Neurons Into Pure Features by Identifying Relevant Circuits
source.authors: Maximilian Dreyer; Erblina Purelku; Johanna Vielhaben; W. Samek; S. Lapuschkin

record.file_problem: Text includes the paper and appendix. Some figures are flattened or illegible in the supplied text.
record.tranche_reason: The paper studies polysemantic neurons in image-classification networks and proposes a circuit-based purification method, but does not test superposition, capacity pressure, or the causal origin of polysemanticity described by the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports CLIP-based clustering results and evaluates PURE against activation-based clustering and DINOv2. The method-comparison results are not recorded as rows because they evaluate the paper's proposed method against alternatives, rather than directly testing a claim version. Cited findings from other work are not recorded.
record.test_reason: The study builds and evaluates a method (PURE) for splitting polysemantic neurons in ImageNet ResNets. It does not cite or test superposition, capacity pressure, toy-model geometry, LLM feature spread, SAE features or feature dimensionality. It hypothesizes that polysemanticity arises from multiple circuits sharing a node, but never tests this against a capacity account. Its ResNet polysemanticity distributions are vision CNNs, not LLMs, and are measured by CLIP separability of top-activating crops, not by dictionary recovery. So no row bears on any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that PURE splits polysemantic neurons into purer virtual neurons by identifying active circuits. They report better CLIP-measured separation than activation-based clustering, close to DINOv2. They make no claims about superposition or capacity.
record.recipe_differences: The paper does not reproduce or apply the Toy Models of Superposition method; it proposes post-hoc clustering of lower-level neuron attributions to assign circuits.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that results hold for k in {3, 4, 5} and other ResNet architectures; it notes that increasing k generally lowers intra-cluster distances but often also lowers inter-cluster distances.

fits_no_version.finding: In ResNet-50's penultimate layer, CLIP-based 2-cluster separability shows a few hundred of 2048 neurons with larger separation. Raising k lowers inter-cluster distance, which the authors read as most neurons being 'rather monosemantic'.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In ImageNet ResNets' penultimate layers, a minority of neurons show visually separable polysemantic reference sets, with the apparent degree possibly varying by architecture.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors hypothesize that polysemanticity arises because multiple circuits share one node. Lower-level attributions cluster into distinct groups for polysemantic neurons, shown qualitatively via UMAP.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Polysemantic neurons in vision CNNs can be decomposed by the distinct upstream circuits active for each feature.

record.problems: The paper treats CLIP and DINOv2 embeddings as proxies for human interpretability and says controlled evaluation or human feedback would be valuable. It also notes that a large ablation study remains for future work. Several plotted values are not legible in the supplied text.
record.rows_left_out: PURE-versus-activation and PURE-versus-DINOv2 comparison outcomes in Figures 4, A.7, and A.8 are omitted: they evaluate the proposed method against alternatives rather than directly testing a claim version. The exact plotted values are not stated in text.

untested.parts: All: no toy models, no sparsity sweep, no geometry of feature directions.
All: no test of whether capacity limits or feature importance determine which neurons are polysemantic.
The circuit-sharing origin of polysemanticity is assumed as a hypothesis, not tested against capacity pressure.
All: no LLMs, no SAE or dictionary recovery.
All: no analysis of feature dimensionality.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T6/discusses call stands; T4 is arguable, since the method presupposes polysemanticity, but superposition itself is never invoked or cited. The method-comparison results are rightly left out as rows. Interpretability is judged by CLIP and DINOv2 proxies, which the authors themselves caveat.

versions.untested_parts: Overcomplete sparse features, overlapping near-orthogonal directions, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry.
Whether feature importance or competition for limited capacity explains dedicated versus shared dimensions.

The paper identifies polysemantic neurons and assigns their semantics to circuits, but does not test whether polysemanticity arises without capacity pressure or whether it is evidence for superposition.
LLMs, neuron-spread measurements, and sparse features recovered by dictionaries or SAEs.
Completeness, stability, or canonical status of SAE features.
Whether represented features are one-dimensional directions or multidimensional.

rows.subject: ResNet-50
rows.operation_detail: Clustered CLIP embeddings of the 100 most activating reference samples per neuron into two clusters; measured overall and inter-/intra-cluster feature-visualization distances.
rows.measure: CLIP embedding distances between feature visualizations; inter-cluster versus intra-cluster distance difference
rows.value: figure only; the text says clustering improves visual similarity for most neurons, with a larger improvement for a few hundred of the 2048 neurons
rows.note: This measures visual separability as a proxy for polysemanticity, but does not test a version's proposed cause or representational geometry.
rows.check: Link to none is correct. This is a CLIP-separability proxy for polysemanticity in a vision CNN and does not measure what any version names. The value is figure-only, apart from the stated 'few hundred of the 2048 neurons'.
